did_you_know.text: The Hebrew word shelamim is related to shalom and the root meaning “wholeness,” suggesting well-being or restored relationship. This offering was also connected with a shared meal for the worshipper and others.
In the Bible, blood is associated with life, so handling it at the altar was a central part of the ritual, not a minor detail. The priests were responsible for carrying out this task.

The phrase “pleasing aroma” is a biblical way of saying that the offering is accepted, not a description of God eating smoke. The Hebrew word ishsheh is generally connected with an offering burned by fire.
The alyah was the sheep’s fat tail, a feature of breeds common in the ancient Near East. The fat stored there served the animal as an important energy reserve.
The phrase “food offering by fire” does not refer to ordinary bread; it is an ancient term for an offering burned on the altar. In biblical Hebrew, the word lechem can also mean food in general.

The ban on eating blood is connected with the idea that blood represents an animal’s life, stated explicitly in Leviticus 17:11. Treating blood with care is therefore not only a dietary rule but also a statement about the sanctity of life.
